items.title: What does it mean for students to do their own work? The issue of originality in the age of AI
items.abstract: If a student uses artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in their work, does that necessarily make the work less “original”? This chapter focuses on the notion of originality and argues for a critical examination of its meaning in a time when AI grows more integrated into students’ work processes. The chapter begins by tracing the historical roots of originality, unpacking how its embedded value orientations around individualism have shaped—and continue to influence—current assessment standards and policies in higher education. It then discusses how these traditional understandings of original work not only are becoming untenable but may also be inadequate for preparing students for a future where AI will significantly shape their way of learning, working, and living. The chapter concludes with several pathways to reimagine originality in higher education assessment, highlighting the need for a more inclusive environment for students to produce meaningful work.

items.title: What is needed for assessment now, and how might GenAI influence this?
items.abstract: The challenge of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provoked a renewed interest in assessment in higher education and how it might need to change. The problems of assessment and the need for repair existed well before AI appeared on the scene, but they are more pressing now. This chapter focuses on the necessary requirements of assessment regardless of the conditions in which it occurs: assessment for assurance; assessment to guide learning; and assessment to build students’ capacity to make evaluative judgements. It examines these purposes and discusses the implications of the rise of GenAI for each. It considers both policies and practices and concludes that, whatever else needs to be done, a priority is to strengthen students’ capacities to make effective evaluative judgements both about their substantive work and about the use of any AI applications that may aid them.

items.abstract: The ubiquity of Large Language Models poses a challenge to student learning in homework-based college courses, where access to easy homework answers devalues the intended productive struggle. To address this concern, we propose Oxbridge-style weekly tutorials, where students present homework problems without notes in a small group with an instructor or TA. We conducted a randomized experiment in an introductory probability class to evaluate the effectiveness of tutorials, finding a significant positive effect of tutorial enrollment on exam grades. We discuss the implementation, challenges, and opportunities in this style of course design.

items.title: When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
items.abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?

items.title: When Humans Still Matter: Consumers’ Responses to Automation in Loyalty Program Preferential Treatment
items.abstract: The recent introduction of automated complimentary upgrades reflects the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI) in making symbolically meaningful decisions in tourism. We explore consumers’ responses using a thematic analysis of online comments and open-ended survey responses, followed by a quantitative survey to validate findings. Paradoxically, the qualitative analysis reveals that both unbiased decisions and personalization are valued. The quantitative study further shows that lay beliefs about AI are associated with preferences, through procedural and interactional fairness. Only procedural fairness fully mediates the lay beliefs’ association with intention to negotiate out of dissatisfying upgrade decisions. Moreover, desire to be treated as a unique customer weakens the lay beliefs’ association with interactional fairness and the indirect association with preferences. We contribute by revealing how consumers respond when automated agents make symbolically meaningful decisions in the automated preferential treatment context. Firms should prioritize the procedural legitimacy and symbolic framing of automated decisions.

items.title: When One AI Model Conducts Others: Where a Fugu-Type Chain Can Slip, and a Warning Number to Catch It Early
items.abstract: Systems such as Sakana AI's Fugu place one coordinating model in front of several other AI models. The coordinator chooses which model works on each step, asks another model to check the work, and merges the results into one answer. This concept note reads the published papers behind such systems (Trinity and the Conductor) and points to seven places where a chain of this kind can slip: the stop decision that rests on one model's judgment, a very delicate reading signal, a coordinator that can call itself, fixed limits that do not show drift, one worker's slip passed to the next step, a pool of models that changes, and a merged answer that carries no sign of how firm it is. The note then suggests a simple, training-free addition: a warning number that measures how slowly the small everyday wobbles of a few signals settle back, read over a series of runs. It is inversely proportional to the size of the leading eigenvalue, so a rising number shows the chain approaching a tipping point. Three calm states follow: Steady, Watch and Look closer. A computer-decided shunting action then acts without waiting for a person. It moves the doubtful runs to a simpler path or an extra check, while all other runs carry on and nothing is stopped. The note describes an idea only. It has not been tested on a real system. Patent pending. items.title: When Seeing Is No Longer Believing: Reddit Users’ Discernment of AI-Generated Visual Content
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly blurs the boundary between real and synthetic visual media, determining whether online content is authentic has become more difficult. This study examines how Reddit users collectively make sense of suspected AI-generated visual content, including images and videos. Rather than assessing detection accuracy, we examine how users judge whether visual content is real or AI-generated. Analyzing 89,697 Reddit comments from AI-focused communities, we identify four major forms of authenticity reasoning: real-world plausibility, visual artifact inspection, source-based assessment, and intuition. Real-world plausibility and visual artifact inspection were the most frequently used strategies, while source-based assessment appeared less often. Authenticity judgments also did not necessarily converge over time. Instead, discussions often diverged as users introduced competing interpretations. These findings suggest that evaluating visual AI-generated content is not simply an individual detection task, but a platformed sensemaking process shaped by users’ reasoning, intuition, and interactions with others.

items.title: When the Artefact Is No Longer Evidence: Assessment Validity and Academic Integrity in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: For most of the history of schooling, producing a piece of work was taken as proof that a learner could do the thinking behind it. Generative AI has broken that assumption. A competent essay, solution or report can now be produced in seconds, and agentic tools can complete whole courses inside a learning platform. Schools and universities have responded mostly by trying to detect AI use, a strategy that research shows is unreliable and biased against non-native English writers. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on detection, assessment validity and high- stakes examinations. It argues that the integrity problem is better understood as a validity problem: the question is not whether a student used AI, but whether an assessment still gives trustworthy evidence of what the student can do. The article sets out the evidence on student use and teacher perceptions, explains why detection fails, describes how single high-stakes examinations have become fragile in 2026, and docu‐ ments assessment designs used in practice, including process portfolios, supervised components, local and personal tasks, oral defence, iterative feedback and source constraints. It proposes an "evidence chain" frame‐ work of five questions that any task should answer, and identifies equity risks in the move to oral and process-based assessment that schools need to manage.

items.title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn't Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks
items.abstract: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

items.title: Whose English Does Generative AI Improve? Algorithmically Mediated Unequal Englishes in the Workplace
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is frequently presented as a linguistic equalizer in workplaces where English mediates recruitment, collaboration, documentation, and customer interaction. Productivity research partly supports this claim, particularly for less-experienced workers. This conceptual piece argues that such gains do not constitute linguistic equality and that, for business communication scholarship, the key issue is how GenAI redistributes communicative authority, adaptation, and credibility within organizations. I call this process Algorithmically Mediated Unequal Englishes (AMUE). It operates through four connected mechanisms: normative compression into AI-polished English, unequal linguistic and affective labor, automated misrecognition and screening, and a credibility trap surrounding authorship and disclosure. These mechanisms offer resources while preserving institutional ‘standards’ and listener expectations. Linguistically equitable AI governance must therefore move beyond providing access to tools. It must redefine effective communication through task relevance, intelligibility, accuracy, reciprocal accommodation, worker control over voice, and institutional responsibility for technological risk.

items.title: Why do students differ in AI competence? Examining the role of attitudes across academic pathways
items.abstract: Students’ attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly recognized as critical drivers of engagement in AI-supported learning. However, the extent to which these attitudes translate into perceived AI competence remains insufficiently understood, particularly within differentiated curricular contexts. Drawing on an integrated Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT) and Opportunity-to-Learn (OTL) perspective, this study examines the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and perceived AI competence and investigates whether this relationship varies across academic tracks. Rather than conceptualizing academic tracks as opportunity-to-learn itself, academic tracks are treated as proxy indicators of differentiated curricular affordances, AI-related exposure, and learning opportunities. AI attitude is conceptualized as a multidimensional construct reflecting exploration, determination, and collaboration, while AI competence captures students’ perceived cognitive, ethical, and applied capabilities in engaging with AI systems. Survey data collected from school students across varied academic tracks were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by Multi-Group Analysis (MGA), endogeneity assessment, and predictive evaluation using PLS-Predict. The findings show that students with more positive attitudes toward AI reported higher perceived AI competence, but this association varied across academic tracks. This suggests that attitudes alone do not translate into competence uniformly; rather, their association with perceived competence may vary according to the learning opportunities available within students’ curricular contexts. Robustness checks indicated no evidence of endogeneity bias and supported the model’s predictive relevance. In essence, the study contributes to AI education research by integrating EVT and OTL into a unified explanatory perspective and by positioning academic tracks as contextual proxies for opportunity-to-learn conditions that shape how students’ value-based engagement develops into AI competence.

items.title: Why Escalate? Typed Escalation for LLM-Judge Panels with Per-Type Conformal Guarantees
items.abstract: LLM judges are increasingly deployed with a reject option. Recent methods certify the error rate of the verdicts these judges accept, but items that are escalated carry no reason, even though conflicting evidence, missing evidence and a false premise call for different remedies. We ask whether a panel of LLM judges can say why it escalates, with a separate statistical guarantee for each reason. Learn-then-Test acceptance is kept, and each escalated item receives a set of escalation types calibrated by per-type split conformal prediction. For each type separately, an escalated item that carries the type includes it with probability at least 0.9 (marginally, for the constructed labels, assuming exchangeable items); for the whole set, only the weaker union bound holds. Typed items were built on SQuAD 2.0 without annotators (conflict, scarcity, both, false premise), and the panel had three judges from different model families (4,801 items). In the preregistered analysis (protocol amended after a pilot that selected the scores), mean per-type coverage over 200 article-level re-partitions was 93.8% (conflict), 91.2% (scarcity) and 94.0% (false premise), and accepted verdicts had a selective risk of 7.5%. Because items are clustered in articles, we added an exploratory article-level variant that is exactly valid when articles are exchangeable. Per-type coverage stayed above 0.9, but sets grew from 1.74 to 1.91 types, and exact article-level acceptance could not be certified with 74 calibration articles. Typed sets contained every true reason for 91.2% of typed escalations; that is higher coverage of reasons, not a measured operational gain. In further exploratory analyses, counting accepted items as misses, end-to-end detection was 42.1%, 69.2% and 35.9%, and on an external false-premise set it was 4.0% and stayed low after recalibration. A supervised score on the same panel outputs gave smaller sets. In an executed retrieval pilot, retrieval resolved most escalations that truly lacked evidence but few others; because the flags put scarcity in most sets, typed routing saved little over retrieving for everything. An automated check by two LLMs flagged 12.9% to 28.5% of conflict labels as doubtful; a human audit is pending. The glut of the existential triple (Dempster’s conflict) was far worse at detecting conflict than asking the judges directly.

items.title: Why Organizational Understanding?
items.abstract: Organizations influence almost every aspect of contemporary life. As employees, managers, customers, citizens, patients, students and members of communities, we constantly interact with organizations that shape opportunities, decisions and outcomes. Understanding organizations, therefore, requires more than examining internal structures and processes; it also requires understanding the broader social, economic, political, technological and cultural contexts in which they operate. This introductory chapter explains why understanding organizations is essential in a world marked by growing complexity, digitalization, artificial intelligence, sustainability challenges and global interdependence. It introduces organization studies as a multidisciplinary field drawing on perspectives from management, sociology, psychology, political science and economics. Key themes include organizations as social systems, value creation, organizational purpose, context, stakeholders and the relationship between organizations and society. By highlighting how organizations both shape and are shaped by their environments, the chapter lays the foundation for the book’s broader exploration of organizational structures, culture, leadership, power, collaboration, change and strategy. It encourages readers to develop analytical insight and critical reflection on organizations in an increasingly interconnected world.

items.title: Wicked solutions
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence poses well-documented challenges for university assessment. Less examined is what happens when expertise about these challenges is brought to bear in practice. Drawing on workshops in which assessment researchers worked with educators redesigning assessments after AI, we show that the advisory encounter broke down in ways we had not previously experienced. Problems refused to stabilise under advice, proposed responses triggered legitimate competing concerns, and no suggestion could obviously produce the closure that educators sought. We argue this reflects a responsibility asymmetry amplified by AI’s particular wickedness. Researchers and other experts can inform judgement but cannot bear the consequences of decisions that educators must enact now, under real institutional and ethical constraints. We call the resulting responses ‘wicked solutions’—not failed advice, but the predictable outcome of offering expert guidance on problems that resist resolution.

items.title: Women's Mental Health and Sustainable Development a Policy and Governance Perspective
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies is reshaping cognitive, emotional, and psychological well-being. This chapter synthesizes interdisciplinary research from psychology, neuroscience, organizational behavior, sociology, and AI ethics to examine how AI-driven environments contribute to anxiety, burnout, technostress, digital fatigue, and emotional strain. It explores the neurobiological and behavioral effects of sustained digital engagement, including disrupted attention, sleep disturbances, and altered decision-making. The chapter highlights the importance of emotional awareness, empathy, and digital self-regulation while arguing that individual resilience alone is insufficient. Aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Goal 3, it advocates systemic reforms in AI design, governance, and institutional practices to support human well-being and sustainable digital futures.

items.title: Worker Welfare and Occupational Health Assurance in Extended-Hours and Night Work on a Saudi Cultural Quarter Development
items.abstract: Large cultural-quarter developments in Saudi Arabia may combine heritage-sensitive construction, multiple contractor interfaces, demanding schedules, and work performed during evening or night hours.These arrangements can reduce daytime heat exposure or public disruption, but may introduce fatigue, circadian disruption, reduced visibility, transport risks, and barriers to accessing health and welfare services.This paper develops an evidence-informed framework for assuring worker welfare and occupational health when extended-hours and night work are used on a Saudi cultural-quarter development.A targeted, nonsystematic synthesis of Saudi regulatory material, international construction-safety guidance, fatigue literature, and Saudi construction heat-stress research informed six assurance pillars: legal and contractual governance; work-time and fatigue control; nightspecific engineering; accessible occupational health and welfare; worker voice and fair treatment; and performance assurance through leading indicators and learning.The paper provides a risk register, implementation roadmap, and monitoring dashboard.It does not report project-level primary data or claim to assess the performance of a named development.The proposed framework should be validated against the current Saudi legal requirements and tested prospectively using project-specific data.

items.abstract: The article examines the economic aspects of applying artificial intelligence technologies and business analytics tools to enhance the profitability of enterprises operating in the field of information and communication technologies (ICT). items.abstract: In the current conditions of digital transformation of society, innovative governance acquires the status of one of the key factors in the modernization of the public administration system. The dynamic development of information and communication technologies, the spread of digital platforms, e-government tools, artificial intelligence, big data and other digital solutions significantly change the mechanisms of interaction between state authorities, local governments, business and civil society. Under these conditions, traditional models of public administration are gradually transforming into more open, adaptive, customer-oriented and innovative governance systems capable of ensuring high quality public services, effective management decision-making and sustainable socio-economic development. In addition, innovative governance is considered as a comprehensive concept that combines modern management approaches, digital technologies, institutional innovations, partnership between authorities, the public and business, as well as mechanisms for joint development and implementation of management decisions. Its implementation contributes to increasing the transparency of government activities, developing open data, ensuring accountability, strengthening citizens' trust in state institutions, and forming an effective public administration system. The paper substantiates that innovative governance is a qualitatively new stage in the development of public administration, characterized by the use of digital technologies to optimize administrative procedures, automate management processes, develop electronic services, ensure transparency and openness of government activities, and expand opportunities for public participation in the formation of public policy. Particular attention is paid to the development of digital platforms for interaction between the state and citizens, the use of open data technologies, e-democracy, digital identification, interagency electronic interaction, as well as the application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and big data analytics technologies in the processes of making management decisions. It is established that the modernization of the public administration system in the context of digitalization involves not only the introduction of modern information technologies, but also a comprehensive reform of the institutional environment, updating regulatory and legal support, the development of digital competencies of civil servants, the formation of an innovative organizational culture, and increasing the level of cybersecurity. At the same time, digital transformation creates new challenges related to personal data protection, digital inequality, information security, the need to ensure the ethical use of artificial intelligence technologies, and guaranteeing the digital rights of citizens. It has been proven that the effective implementation of innovative governance ensures increased efficiency of public authorities, reduction of administrative costs, optimization of administrative service provision processes, increased efficiency of management decisions, expansion of opportunities for public participation and strengthening of democratic governance. Of particular importance is the integration of the principles of openness, transparency, accountability, partnership, innovation and people-centeredness into the functioning of the modern public administration system.

items.abstract: The article examines the transformation of the thematic landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) in management and identifies its structural changes. The empirical basis of the study comprises metadata from scientific articles indexed in the Scopus database and selected using the PRISMA methodology. The methodological framework combines bibliometric analysis, keyword co-occurrence analysis, network visualization, thematic clustering, and a comparison of the absolute and relative representation of research clusters across the periods 2019–2022 and 2023–2025. The findings reveal an acceleration in research on AI in management, accompanied by a broader thematic scope and an expansion of international research collaboration. Network analysis identified four interconnected thematic clusters covering technological and analytical support for managerial decision-making; human resource, knowledge, and organizational process management; operations, project, and risk management; and responsible AI governance, ethics, and regulation. Strong interconnections between these clusters indicate the gradual emergence of an integrated approach to studying AI in management. The comparison between the two periods reveals a structural reconfiguration of research priorities: while all thematic areas demonstrate absolute growth, the relative dominance of technology-oriented research has declined, whereas attention to organizational, human, ethical, and regulatory dimensions has increased. Particularly dynamic growth is observed in research related to generative AI, human–AI interaction, innovation, digital transformation, sustainability, and responsible management. The findings demonstrate an evolutionary shift in research focus from the technological and operational application of AI toward its managerial and organizational integration, followed by the emergence of responsible and human-centered approaches. The results provide a foundation for further research on managerial capabilities for AI integration, models of interaction between humans and intelligent systems, and mechanisms for the responsible use of AI.

items.title: "Uso de Tecnologías de la Información y la Comunicación (TIC) y su Asociación con las Dimensiones del Pensamiento Crítico en Discentes de Educación Superior: Un Estudio Mixto Explicativo"
items.abstract: Título: Uso de Tecnologías de la Información y la Comunicación (TIC) y su Asociación con las Dimensiones del Pensamiento Crítico en Discentes de Educación Superior: Un Estudio Mixto Explicativo Antecedentes: En la era digital, la omnipresencia de las Tecnologías de la Información y la Comunicación (TIC) y la irrupción de la Inteligencia Artificial Generativa (IAGen) han transformado los entornos de aprendizaje en salud. En el Internado Rotatorio de Pregrado, el personal médico en adiestramiento enfrenta una constante sobrecarga informativa (infoxicación) e interacción con herramientas automatizadas. Un uso puramente instrumental o delegativo de las TIC puede comprometer el desarrollo de competencias cognitivas de orden superior, mientras que un uso epistémico puede potenciar el análisis, la inferencia, la evaluación y la autorregulación clínica. Objetivo: Determinar la asociación entre los patrones de uso de las TIC (incluyendo la IAGen y la alfabetización informacional) y el nivel de desarrollo de las dimensiones del pensamiento crítico en Médicos Internos de Pregrado (MIP) en unidades de segundo nivel de atención del IMSS, e interpretar los procesos metacognitivos subyacentes desde la perspectiva estudiantil. Material y Métodos: Estudio mixto con Diseño Secuencial Explicativo (DEXPLI). · Fase 1 (Cuantitativa): Diseño multicéntrico, observacional, transversal y analítico en tres sedes (HGZ No. 53, HGZ No. 197 y HGZ No. 71, OOAD Estado de México Oriente). Se incluirá por censo a la plantilla total de MIP. Se aplicará la Escala Multidimensional de Patrones de Uso de TIC (\alpha = 0.87) y un cuestionario estandarizado de dimensiones de Pensamiento Crítico (Facione). Se realizarán análisis descriptivos, correlación de Pearson, ANOVA multicéntrico y modelos de Regresión Lineal Múltiple. · Fase 2 (Cualitativa): Abordaje fenomenológico interpretativo mediante 4 grupos focales (n = 32 MIP) estructurados por muestreo intencional de casos extremos según los cuartiles de desempeño de la Fase 1 (Q_1 y Q_4). Los testimonios serán transcritos y analizados categorialmente mediante codificación temática en ATLAS.ti para triangular las meta-inferencias. Resultados Esperados: Se prevé identificar una asociación positiva y estadísticamente significativa entre el uso epistémico de TIC/IAGen y puntajes elevados en las dimensiones de análisis, inferencia y autorregulación. Asimismo, se espera caracterizar cómo la delegación cognitiva pasiva se vincula con un menor rendimiento crítico y cómo la alfabetización informacional mitiga la infoxicación en la toma de decisiones clínicas. Conclusiones: La investigación aportará evidencia empírica clave para la optimización tecno-pedagógica de los planes de estudio del Internado Rotatorio, permitiendo establecer lineamientos éticos y metodológicos para la integración reflexiva de las TIC e IAGen en el IMSS. Palabras Clave (DeCS): Tecnología de la Información; Pensamiento; Educación Médica; Inteligencia Artificial; Internado y Residencia; Toma de Decisiones Clínicas. Structured Abstract (English) Title: Use of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) and Its Association with Critical Thinking Dimensions in Higher Education Students: An Explanatory Mixed-Methods Study Background: In the digital era, the ubiquity of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) and the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) have reshaped medical learning environments. During Undergraduate Rotating Internship, medical interns face continuous information overload (infoxication) and interaction with automated tools. A purely instrumental or delegative use of ICT may hinder high-order cognitive development, whereas epistemic use can foster clinical analysis, inference, evaluation, and self-regulation. Objective: To determine the association between ICT usage patterns (including GenAI and information literacy) and the development level of critical thinking dimensions in Undergraduate Medical Interns (MIP) across second-level IMSS hospitals, and to interpret underlying metacognitive processes from the students' perspective. Material and Methods: A mixed-methods study with an Explanatory Sequential Design (DEXPLI). · Phase 1 (Quantitative): Multicenter, observational, cross-sectional, analytical study across three sites (General Zone Hospital No. 53, No. 197, and No. 71, OOAD Estado de México Oriente). Total population sampling of active interns will be conducted. Instruments: Multidimensional ICT Usage Patterns Scale (\alpha = 0.87) and a standardized Critical Thinking Dimensions Scale (Facione). Statistical analysis: descriptive metrics, Pearson correlation, multicenter ANOVA, and Multiple Linear Regression models. · Phase 2 (Qualitative): Interpretive phenomenological approach using 4 focus groups (n = 32 interns) selected via purposive extreme-case sampling based on Phase 1 performance quartiles (Q_1 and Q_4). Focus group transcripts will undergo thematic analysis and matrix coding using ATLAS.ti to build integrated meta-inferences. Expected Results: We expect to demonstrate a statistically significant positive association between epistemic ICT/GenAI usage and higher scores in analysis, inference, and self-regulation. Additionally, qualitative analysis will elucidate how passive cognitive delegation links to lower critical performance and how information literacy buffers infoxication during clinical decision-making. Conclusions: This study will provide key empirical evidence to optimize techno-pedagogical curricula for medical internships, informing institutional policies and ethical guidelines for the reflective integration of ICT and GenAI within IMSS training programs. items.title: 360° MDL: The Multidimensional Literature Review Model — Version 2026
items.abstract: 360° MDL (the Multidimensional Literature Review Model) is a methodology for conducting and reporting literature reviews that create value, not just volume. It tells researchers where to look (five evidence stream families: academic databases, influential scholars, industry practice, policy and global organisations, and emerging and diverse voices), what to keep (the 6R Quality Gate and CCD Curation for Complementarity, Coverage and Diversity), how to analyse (eight standard analysis matrices, M1–M8), how sure to be (Triangulation Strength, Resilience Index and a Leave-One-Stream-Out test) and what value to create (Interpretation & Exploitation and an evidence-traced Value-Based Framework). The methodology comes in three tiers: Lite for doctoral students and thesis chapters, Standard for journal review articles, and Advanced for flagship and policy reviews. All three share the 3 × 3 Rule: at least three source streams × at least three analysis matrices. It includes a 30-item reporting checklist (MDL-RC 2026) and a flow diagram compatible with PRISMA 2020, so it complements PRISMA rather than replacing it. This release contains:• Methodology Overview: the full description of the method• Researcher Handbook: step-by-step guidelines, rubrics, checklists and a protocol template• Quick Start Guide and one-page Quick Reference Card: a ready-to-use route in 10 steps for researchers and doctoral students• Excel Toolkit (blank and a worked example) with live calculation of all indices• 24 figures (PNG and vector PDF) and an illustrative example review on smart cities About the author: Professor Miltiadis D. Lytras is Full Professor of Information Systems and Digital Transformation at Deree, The American University of Greece, and Research Professor at Effat University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. He holds a BSc in Informatics, an MBA and a PhD in Knowledge Management and e-Learning from the Athens University of Economics and Business. His research spans knowledge management, data science, artificial intelligence, the semantic web, technology-enhanced learning and digital transformation. He has served as Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal on Semantic Web and Information Systems, has guest-edited more than 85 special issues in Web of Science-indexed journals, and has authored or edited more than 80 international books. He has been listed among the world's top computer scientists by Guide2Research and among leading scientists in the AD Scientific Index, and he has served as Distinguished Scientist at King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah. 360° MDL distils more than two decades of his experience in editing, reviewing and writing literature reviews into an open, citable methodology. How to cite: Lytras, M. D. (2026). 360° MDL: The Multidimensional Literature Review Model — Version 2026. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23724393 Researchers who use the methodology are invited to state in their methods section: "This review was conducted and reported according to the 360° MDL methodology, Version 2026 (Lytras, 2026)."

items.title: A 211K Parameter Foundation Model: Genetic Prompting in Neural Cellular Automata
items.abstract: The scale of modern foundation models enables broad task generalization. In medical imaging, where segmentation demands vary widely across clinical contexts, such flexibility is invaluable. But current models, such as SAM trade adaptability for scale, locking their utility behind high-end infrastructure and leaving behind the low-resource environments most in need of diagnostic support. To bridge this gap, we introduce Foundational-NCA, a lightweight foundation model capable of adapting to a wide range of medical segmentation tasks without retraining. Built on Neural Cellular Automata (NCA), Foundational-NCA incorporates gradient-based learning with genetic optimization over a latent task space, using a compact task vector to guide predictions. This enables dynamic adaptation via a genetic prompt mechanism, allowing the model to generalize across tasks while keeping the parameter count magnitudes lower at just 211 thousand, compared to SAM-based models with 38.9 to 636 million parameters. We evaluate Foundational-NCA on 15 trained and 6 entirely unseen segmentation tasks from the TotalSegmentator dataset, achieving an average Dice score of 84.5% on known tasks and 60.4% on unseen ones. These results demonstrate that task generalization is possible in ultra-compact models, laying the groundwork for resource-efficient, deployable foundation models in clinical environments where infrastructure is limited. By reducing model size by over 180 times, Foundational-NCA takes a step toward a more equitable future for medical AI, one where powerful tools are within reach of every healthcare setting.

items.title: A 4D reconstruction of ancient Troy with AI-assisted interpretive interaction
items.abstract: This paper presents a phase-based, real-time four-dimensional (4D) reconstruction of ancient Troy, enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted interpretive interaction with selected virtual characters. Defined by nine superimposed settlement layers, Troy presents particular challenges for conventional two-dimensional (2D) documentation and static three-dimensional (3D) representations, especially when communicating long-term urban transformation to specialist and non-specialist audiences. To address this challenge, all nine principal phases were reconstructed as spatially aligned but separately managed layers within a single Unreal Engine 5 environment. Excavation records, stratigraphic documentation, published archaeological interpretations, and architectural reference drawings were converted into evidence-based 3D models in Autodesk 3ds Max and optimized for real-time visualization. The interpretive component uses retrieval-grounded generative conversational AI, implemented through Convai, for selected phase-aware non-player characters (NPCs). Each character is linked to curated, phase-specific historical knowledge and constrained by a defined speaking scope, contextual prompts, and response rules. The AI was not used to generate archaeological geometry, determine architectural form, or create unrestricted historical narratives. Instead, it supports contextual explanation, visitor orientation, educational mediation, and phase-specific readability while remaining subordinate to the archaeological evidence. The workflow also separates documented, inferred, and speculative elements so that uncertainty can be communicated without presenting every visual decision as equally certain. The project demonstrates that a phase-based real-time environment, combined with carefully bounded conversational AI and virtual reality (VR) interaction, can improve comparative understanding of a multi-layer archaeological site while maintaining archaeological traceability, technical performance, and interpretative transparency. Furthermore, the proposed workflow establishes a reproducible framework for integrating archaeological documentation, immersive visualization, and AI-assisted interpretation within a single interactive environment. By allowing users to examine each settlement phase independently while preserving their spatial correspondence, the system facilitates clearer observation of architectural continuity and transformation over time while supporting transparent scholarly communication, heritage education, future comparative research, and informed public engagement.

items.title: A Case Study of a Multi-Agent Kernel-Optimization Loop That Learns a New AI Accelerator
items.abstract: Frontier large language models write correct CUDA kernels for most single-operator benchmark tasks, yet their accuracy collapses on accelerators whose architecture and programming language they have rarely seen. We present a case study of an LLM agent loop built for such accelerators. Our example is the FuriosaAI RNGD NPU, programmed in a recent, sparsely documented Rust DSL, where the loop optimized three Gemma-4-12B decode kernels over 12 days on a shared, scarce device. The loop builds its own target knowledge: it writes and checks a summary of the DSL documentation, measures the chip with microbenchmarks, records compiler-derived legality rules, and revisits this knowledge when the toolchain changes, rechecking rules and measurements where it can. A role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees explores whole-kernel designs and accumulates small accepted changes in the best version of each kernel. Because device time is scarce and readings are noisy, cheap checks screen new designs before any device run, and late in the run a change was accepted only after repeated comparisons with the best kernel on the device. The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline, each within 1.25x of the cycles needed just to move its weights. Our prompts, profiler and acceptance test are available at https://github.com/bgchun-fs/multi-agent-kernel-gen-loop.

items.title: A Comprehensive Review of Transfer Learning-Based Sentiment Analysis Using BERT and Transformer Models
items.abstract: Sentiment analysis is a task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that detects polarity, opinions, emotions, or attitudes in text data. Traditional systems based on lexicons and hand-crafted features are relatively straightforward, but their adaptability is constrained by vocabulary, context, domain differences, and linguistic variation. Deep learning introduced CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU, and attention-based representations, while transformer-based pre-trained language models significantly improved contextual transfer. Transfer learning reduces the cost of target-domain annotation by leveraging knowledge from a source domain or a pre-trained model for a target sentiment task. This review examines transfer-learning methods for sentiment analysis, focusing on machine learning, artificial intelligence, natural language processing, Hugging Face Transformers, BERT, and the fine-tuning of pre-trained language models. The literature is organized into transfer-learning taxonomy, model development, BERT-based modifications, hybrid architectures, datasets, evaluation approaches, limitations, and emerging parameter-efficient techniques. The analysis highlights research gaps in source-domain selection, negative-transfer detection, low-resource and code-mixed evaluation, computational efficiency, explainability, continual adaptation, and reproducibility. The review suggests that promising future systems should not focus solely on increasing model size, but should identify relevant knowledge, adapt effectively, and maintain robustness across diverse domains and languages.

items.title: A Conceptual Research on Responsible Artificial Intelligence and Ethical Business Practices
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of routine business judgment. Firms use it to identify customers, screen job applicants, anticipate demand, evaluate credit and prepare managerial reports. These applications promise speed and scale. They also create difficult questions about fairness, privacy, worker dignity, accountability and the public consequences of automated decisions. This conceptual paper examines how responsible artificial intelligence can be translated into ethical business practices rather than treated as a separate compliance exercise. Drawing on recent peer-reviewed research published primarily between 2024 and 2026, the discussion connects stakeholder responsibility, organizational governance and the practical management of AI systems. It identifies six business-facing ethical obligations and develops a proposed framework linking leadership commitment, risk-sensitive design, human oversight, stakeholder voice and continuing assurance to ethical outcomes. The paper argues that a responsible firm does more than publish AI principles. It determines where AI should be used, records who remains answerable for each decision and creates a workable route for challenge and correction. The framework is presented as a set of conceptual propositions for subsequent empirical testing. Implications are discussed for managers, auditors, policymakers and smaller firms with limited technical capacity. The central conclusion is that responsible AI is best understood as an ongoing organizational capability that protects human interests while enabling legitimate business innovation

items.title: A Declaration on Power, Freedom, and the Public Nature of Intelligence in the Age of AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves into a foundational infrastructure of future civilization, concerns surrounding AI governance extend beyond technological capability and existential risk. This declaration argues that the defining challenge of the AI era lies in the potential concentration of intelligence infrastructure and the resulting concentration of cognitive influence within a limited number of technological ecosystems. While vertically integrated AI systems may accelerate innovation, they may also create new forms of structural dependence that threaten individual and societal freedom. To address these emerging risks, the paper introduces three interrelated concepts: Technological Sovereignty, defined as freedom from dependence on a single technological ecosystem; Cognitive Sovereignty, understood as the ability to maintain meaningful control over one's own processes of thought and judgment; and Ontological Autonomy, the capacity to remain the author of one's own existence in an increasingly AI-mediated world. Building upon the framework of On-Site Adaptive Innovation (OAI), the declaration emphasizes the importance of decentralized adaptive capabilities and the democratization of intelligence infrastructure. It concludes that the future of AI will be shaped not only by the power of intelligent systems but also by the governance structures that determine access to and control of intelligence itself. Preserving technological plurality, cognitive freedom, and human autonomy is therefore presented as a fundamental prerequisite for maintaining freedom in the age of artificial intelligence.

items.title: A Deep Learning and Digital Twin Framework for Automated Crack Detection and Maintenance-Oriented Condition Assessment of Industrial Buildings
items.abstract: The maintenance of industrial buildings is essential to ensure the operability, safety, and efficiency of these facilities, which are key pillars of the industrial sector. Proper maintenance management has a direct impact on productivity and the continuity of operational processes. However, managing the maintenance of these built assets pose significant challenges, particularly in terms of efficiency in inspection, diagnosis, and the planning of corrective and preventive activities, requiring substantial investment to preserve functionality and prevent disruptions. To address these challenges, this paper presents the development of an intelligent system for advanced damage diagnosis in industrial buildings. The system integrates the MIVES multi-criteria decision-making methodology to objectively assess the structural condition of built assets, incorporating complementary technologies: drones for inspection; artificial intelligence (AI) for data analysis and automatic damage detection; extended reality (XR) for the relocalisation of previously captured environments and the spatial positioning of identified damage; and radiance fields (such as 3D Gaussian Splatting) for 3D scene reconstruction and digital twin generation. A prototype workflow for damage detection was developed by training deep-learning algorithms trained on field images of pathologies in industrial built assets and generating digital twins of the facility using photogrammetry techniques and 3D Gaussian Splatting. This workflow supports the detection and visualization of potential pathologies and provides the data necessary for their objective assessment within the MIVES-base condition condition-assessment framework. These developments are integrated into an application that allows managers and asset owners to access and track inspection information through structured damage records, spatial localization, and digital visualization tools that support maintenance planning and decision-making.

items.title: A Defense-Aware Explainable AI Framework for Feature-Level Vulnerability Analysis in Optimal Power Flow
items.abstract: Optimal power flow (OPF) is a foundational analysis in power system operation, and inaccuracies in OPF decision-making can result in significant operational and security consequences. With the increasing adoption of machine-learning-based OPF surrogate models for real-time and large-scale applications, power system operation has become more susceptible to cyber threats, including data manipulation and false data injection attacks. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), particularly Shapley value-based approaches, has been employed to quantify the influence of input features on OPF outputs. Features exhibiting high influence are commonly interpreted as vulnerable. However, this interpretation neglects the role of attack detection mechanisms in the system, which typically monitor input-to-input relationships to detect anomalous behavior. Consequently, highly influential features may be readily detectable and may not represent the most vulnerable attack surfaces. To address this limitation, we propose a defense-aware explainable AI framework that explicitly incorporates attack detectability alongside operational impact. The framework integrates an OPF surrogate model representing input-to-output dependencies with a vanilla autoencoder representing input-to-input dependencies. Shapley-based explainability is applied to both models to construct a feature-level vulnerability metric. Empirical evaluation on IEEE test systems demonstrates that the proposed framework more accurately identifies security-relevant vulnerabilities than conventional OPF-surrogate-model-only explainability approaches.

items.title: A Framework for Identifying and Understanding Cognitive Biases in Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Radiology
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) creates new susceptibility to diagnostic error in radiology related to the cognitive processes by which radiologists' interpretations incorporate AI outputs. This Perspective presents a conceptual framework for cognitive biases in AI-assisted radiology linking specific biases to radiologist-AI interactions. The framework uses dual-process theory, recognizing fast intuitive and deliberate analytic modes of information processing, as an organizing model for understanding cognitive processes underlying radiologists' decisions and their potential contribution to bias. Across seven decision scenarios spanning image viewing, findings interpretation, and contextual integration, the framework examines how AI output timing, radiologist-AI agreement, trust calibration, and reader expertise influence decision-making. We identify adaptive heuristics that support efficient decisions but, when misapplied or overrelied upon, increase susceptibility to complacency, confirmation, automation, distrust, anchoring, and usual implication bias, and increase behavioral risk of use without qualification. We highlight AI paradoxes emerging from the framework of despecialization, system fragility, and deskilling. Finally, we propose strategies targeting these cognitive biases, including education and experiential learning, workflow and interface design, clinical oversight, and performance monitoring. This framework provides a structured basis for generating testable hypotheses and designing AI-assisted radiology systems that preserve the strengths of human expertise and AI while supporting calibrated reliance.

items.title: A generalizable 3D dose prediction across heterogeneous cohorts: A framework developed for the 2025 AAPM GDP‐HMM challenge
items.abstract: Abstract Background Manual radiotherapy treatment planning is labor‐intensive, subjective, and highly variable across planners and institutions. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach for estimating achievable three‐dimensional (3D) dose distributions for a given plan (hereafter: dose prediction) by directly mapping patient anatomy and beam geometry to voxel‐wise dose. However, achieving robust generalization across diverse anatomical sites, prescriptions, and institutions remains a major challenge, particularly under computational constraints required for clinical deployment. Purpose We sought to develop and evaluate a generalizable, computationally efficient 3D dose prediction framework capable of spanning heterogeneous multi‐site and multi‐cohort datasets, as defined in the 2025 AAPM Generalizable Dose Prediction for Heterogeneous Multi‐Cohort and Multi‐Site (GDP‐HMM) Grand Challenge. Our goal was to design a model that not only achieved state‐of‐the‐art voxel‐wise accuracy but also maintained clinically meaningful dose‐volume and geometric characteristics across diverse cases. Methods We implemented a fully convolutional 3D dose‐prediction model adapted from the MedNeXt architecture, which was originally introduced as a high‐capacity convolutional backbone for medical image segmentation and is well suited to volumetric dense prediction tasks. The network accepted multimodal inputs comprising CT, PTV/OAR masks, beam and angle plates, and scalar plan metadata. A composite loss function combined voxel‐wise L 1 , body‐masked weighted L 1 , structure‐wise moment‐matching, and gradient‐based penalties to jointly preserve spatial fidelity and dosimetric accuracy. The model was trained on the fixed GDP‐HMM dataset consisting of 2876 training plans, 356 validation plans, and a held‐out test set of 498 plans using random 3D patches and evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE), homogeneity index (HI), and conformity indices (CI100%, CI50%). Ablation studies quantified the contribution of each loss component to overall performance. Statistical comparisons used paired Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction. Results The proposed model achieved a mean voxel‐wise MAE of 2.04 Gy on the validation set, outperforming the challenge baseline (2.54 Gy). An ensemble with the baseline further improved MAE to 1.94 Gy on the validation set and 2.071 Gy on the held‐out test set, corresponding to the lowest test‐set MAE and first‐place overall ranking in the GDP‐HMM Challenge. Predicted dose distributions preserved key plan characteristics, with ΔHI, ΔCI 100% , and ΔCI 50% narrowly centered around zero, indicating consistent target coverage and dose conformity. Protocol‐specific evaluations for head‐and‐neck and lung cohorts demonstrated close alignment with reference plans, with no systematic degradation in OAR endpoints. Ablation experiments showed that removing gradient‐based terms increased MAE by 0.50 Gy, while excluding the moment‐matching term increased MAE by 0.06 Gy confirming that both gradient‐ and moment‐based constraints enhanced spatial and dosimetric fidelity. Conclusion We present a generalizable 3D dose prediction framework that achieves state‐of‐the‐art accuracy while satisfying stringent runtime requirements (< 3s per case on < 24 GB GPU memory). By integrating gradient‐aware and moment‐based constraints within a MedNeXt backbone, the model preserved clinical DVH endpoints and geometric plan features. These findings demonstrate that carefully engineered loss formulations are pivotal for cross‐institutional generalization. The framework offers a foundation for rapid dose prediction that could accelerate treatment planning, reduce inter‐planner variability, and enable intelligent automation in radiotherapy workflows.

items.title: A Human-Stiffness-Based Simulator for Ergonomic Evaluation of Pistol-Grip Power Tool Reaction
items.abstract: Powered pistol-grip fastening tools can produce substantial handle rotation during torque build-up, which may contribute to operator overuse injuries. This study developed and evaluated a human-stiffness-based physical simulator for a controlled relative comparison of fastening variables affecting peak handle rotation. The simulator used a DC-powered pistol-grip tool, which was constrained to rotate about its spindle axis, with a double-acting pneumatic cylinder providing resistance set according to a specified human-derived stiffness. The evaluation used stiffness data from 10 operators at 5 and 7.5 N·m, with simulator peak displacement compared to in vivo measurements using paired analyses. The simulator was then used as a screening platform to examine the effect of target torque and, at 7.5 N·m, the effects of fastener material, drive style, head type, and spindle speed. The simulator overpredicted human peak displacement, with mean biases of 14.72° at 5 N·m and 10.29° at 7.5 N·m. The peak rotation increased by 15.0% when torque was increased from 5 to 7.5 N·m (p = 0.022). Torx Plus style fasteners produced 11.5% less rotation than Hex drive fasteners; fastener material significantly affected rotation; head type did not; and rotation was substantially lower at 160 rpm. Although the simulator did not reproduce absolute human displacement without bias, the results support its use as a screening platform for relative comparison under fixed mechanical boundary conditions rather than as an absolute predictor of human displacement or injury risk.

items.title: A Landscape Review of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Enabled Teacher Professional Development at Scale
items.abstract: Teacher Professional Development (TPD) significantly influences student learning, yet implementing equitable, quality, and efficient TPD at scale remains a persistent challenge. Emerging technologies—particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI)—offer promising avenues for addressing tensions between localisation and personalisation, but a comprehensive understanding of AI’s role in scaling in-service TPD remains lacking. Guided by the overarching question of how AI enables in-service TPD to be implemented at scale with equity, quality, and efficiency, this landscape review examines three research questions: how AI-enabled TPD programmes address equity, quality, and efficiency at scale; what roles AI plays in enabling TPD at scale; and what promising practices and lessons emerge from such programmes. The review draws conceptually on the World Bank Group’s Technology for Teaching (T4T) framework, which delineates three sequential stages of technology-enhanced TPD: Access, Engage, and Apply. Sources included peer-reviewed studies, policy documents, and grey literature with a pre-defined typology. From an initial pool of 576 articles, 504 were screened after removing duplicates; 34 articles directly addressing the research questions underwent full-text review, supplemented by 59 partially aligned sources. Findings indicate that AI-enabled TPDs address equity, quality, and efficiency at scale by expanding equitable access for teachers of less mainstream K-12 subjects and geographically distant populations while supporting teacher retention by fostering meaningful learning and reducing administrative burden. Regarding roles that AI plays in enabling TPD at scale, AI’s principal affordances include expanding teachers’ knowledge base and learning assets, functioning as a personalised learning coach, and supporting classroom learning management beyond the TPD itself. Common practices that are tentatively effective emerged from the findings include AI chatbots, AI-assisted evaluation reports, and AI-enabled automation, with strong AI-capable leadership emerging as a potentially critical enabler. This review paper also provided practical implications for TPD practitioners, as well as directions for future research. The review’s primary limitations include the scarcity of global research on the topic, the threat of knowledge coloniality, and language constraints that affect the availability and validity of documentation.

items.title: A Large Language Model–Guided Q‐Learning Method for Food Safety Sampling Decision‐Making
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Food safety sampling is a critical measure for safeguarding public health; however, current regulatory practices are challenged by fragmented risk signals, constrained inspection resources, and suboptimal inspection efficiency. To address these issues, this paper proposes a food safety sampling decision‐making method based on large language models (LLM)–guided Q‐learning. First, we leverage LLMs to extract and analyze key elements from unstructured online food safety public opinion data. This is integrated with clustering analysis and the entropy weight method to achieve quantitative risk assessment and grading. Subsequently, a food category–region risk score matrix is constructed, and the allocation of sampling frequency is formalized as a sequential decision‐making problem under resource constraints. Q‐learning is then introduced to learn optimal sampling strategies, using LLM‐generated structured heuristic values as prior guidance, thereby reducing ineffective exploration and enhancing training efficiency. Experimental results, based on data from 30 provincial administrative regions, 457 municipalities/counties, and 25 food categories, generated 4690 risk evaluation records as effective inputs for decision‐making. The results demonstrate that the derived sampling strategies align with risk priors, allocating higher sampling intensity to high‐risk food category–region combinations while maintaining coverage balance across food categories and regions. Compared to the baseline without heuristic guidance, LLM guidance significantly reduces convergence iterations while maintaining steady‐state rewards. This indicates that the proposed method accelerates policy learning without compromising long‐term returns. In conclusion, this study validates that the proposed method achieves a closed‐loop integration of risk assessment and decision optimization, providing a data‐driven methodology for intelligent food safety regulation.

items.title: A longitudinal case study of practice and policy gaps in responsible AI adoption across Ukrainian higher education from 2023 to 2025
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) entered Ukrainian higher education during a period of unprecedented institutional disruption: full-scale war, infrastructure loss, and emergency distance learning. Two annual faculty surveys conducted by the Marketers Association of Ukraine in June 2023 (n=65, 30 higher-education institutions) and June-August 2024 (n=82, 35 higher-education institutions) document a rapid bottom-up uptake that outpaced any institutional governance response, until April 2025, when the Ministry of Digital Transformation, the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, the United Kingdom's International Development programme, and the Eurasia Foundation jointly issued national Recommendations on the responsible implementation and use of artificial intelligence technologies in higher-education institutions. The recommendations anchor higher-education AI governance in the seven trustworthy-AI principles of the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group (human oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; accountability) and add academic integrity as an eighth, sector-specific principle. This paper uses the two surveys, conducted before the policy existed, as a baseline-fidelity measurement against those eight dimensions. We construct a practice-policy fidelity matrix mapping survey items to policy dimensions, score per-dimension fidelity for the 2024 cohort, and segment results by academic rank, discipline, and institutional ISO 31000 risk-management adoption. Baseline fidelity is low across the six dimensions with survey proxies (mean 0.227, range 0.092 to 0.293); the steepest gap is on accountability, the dimension named highest-risk by the EU AI Act for educational use. Two dimensions (diversity/non-discrimination; societal/environmental well-being) have no item proxy in the 2024 instrument and are explicit data gaps for any successor wave. Witnessed student academic-integrity violations rose from 40.0% in 2023 to 52.4% in 2024 against essentially flat policy coverage. We compare Ukrainian patterns against contemporary international evidence on faculty GenAI adoption (Saudi, Romanian, Turkish, Indian, Thai, and US studies) and propose a sequenced implementation pathway addressing the steepest-gradient dimensions first. The paper contributes the first peer-reviewed longitudinal evidence on Ukrainian higher-education AI adoption during the 2022-2025 war and a reusable fidelity-matrix methodology for benchmarking practice against national responsible-AI frameworks.

items.title: A model for enhancing the quality of geography education based on the integration of Artificial Intelligence and Geographic Information Systems
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) is increasingly central to improving the quality of geography education. This study developed a model intended for enhancing geography education quality based on AI-GIS integration and empirically examined future geography teachers’ readiness to adopt these technologies, drawing on a survey of 100 bachelor's, master's, and doctoral students in geography at al-Farabi Kazakh National University (27 items across three blocks: socio-intellectual characteristics, experience and integration, and professional/ethical issues; Cronbach's α = 0.78, χ 2 (3) = 24.56, p < 0.001). Sixty-seven percent of students reported readiness to use AI-GIS technologies (12% fully ready, 55% ready but requiring further training), and an equal share wished to develop their knowledge in this area further; familiarity was higher for AI (68%) than for GIS (26%) or GeoAI (8%); 99% had used ChatGPT or a similar tool, and ArcGIS was the most common GIS platform (66%). Readiness to use the technologies was associated with GIS familiarity ( ρ = 0.51), GIS proficiency ( ρ = 0.47), and GeoAI knowledge ( ρ = 0.43), but not with general AI familiarity ( ρ = 0.07); H3 and H4 were supported, H1 was not, and H2 was reported as a descriptive result. Although 88% of students viewed AI-GIS integration as beneficial to instructional quality, 67% were unaware of algorithmic bias issues and only 6% had applied these technologies in teaching practice. The results informed a proposed five-component model (content, technological, methodological, integrative, and competency) that has not yet been tested empirically. It is intended for improving teacher-training programs, designing practical courses, and developing future teachers’ digital competence, critical thinking, and ethical awareness.

items.title: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Dynamic Constitutional (Prakriti) Profiling and Personalized Ayurvedic Interventions
items.abstract: Traditional Ayurvedic diagnostics rely on determining an individual's baseline constitution (Prakriti) and acute functional imbalances (Vikriti) through qualitative clinical evaluations and longitudinal lifestyle assessments. While foundational to personalized holistic care, manual constitutional profiling exhibits inter-practitioner variability, requires substantial clinical time, and lacks continuous adaptability to acute physiological or environmental shifts. This paper presents a Multi-Agent Large Language Model (LLM) and Rule-Hybrid Architecture designed to structure constitutional classification and generate source-grounded lifestyle (Vihara), dietary (Ahara), and botanical (Aushadha) educational recommendations. By decoupling diagnostic sub-tasks across specialized cooperative agents and enforcing a deterministic rule-verification engine, the proposed framework separates stable baseline traits from transient symptom fluctuations while constraining unsupported generative outputs. Evaluated on a held-out synthetic benchmark cohort of 200 multi-modal profiles (derived from a 250-profile curated dataset) labeled by a consensus panel of three certified Ayurvedic physicians, the framework achieves an overall classification accuracy of 90.0%, a macro-F1 score of 0.892, and a system-to-consensus Cohen's kappa of κ=0.863(95% CI: 0.808–0.918). Ablation experiments against deterministic rule baselines and monolithic single-LLM configurations demonstrate that multi-agent task separation combined with deterministic safety gating eliminates 100.0% of predefined contraindication rule violations across benchmark and adversarial stress tests. Adhering to TRIPOD+AI reporting standards, we detail the knowledge-base provenance, system failure modes, computational overhead, and human-in-the-loop governance required for responsible deployment in integrative health informatics. items.title: A Pedagogical Framework Based on Design Dissection to Drive Innovation in Technically Complex Product Design Education
items.abstract: Designing innovative products integrated with technically complex product de- sign focused on user centric remains a significant challenges in design education. Product dissec- tion has been utilized as one of the efficient methods to interact the products to understand its working principle and to generate creative outcomes. The proposed pedagogical framework focus mainly on the functional understanding of the product being dissected. The purpose of the pro- posed work is to investigate the effectiveness of the students learning rate with respect to the product types such as mechanical, and electrical. The approach of the investigation deals with the design dissection of various products as a core teaching methods. The application of particular design thinking methods such as SCAMPER, and Morphological Matrix as blend with design dissection increase the creative outcomes. Technical realizability, ergonomic, user experience, compliance with standard and novelty are the metrics to evaluate the design outcomes. Better understanding of the various domain principles of components with functional complexities leads to innovative concepts and new product design. The findings from this investigation expose the understanding of products through the design dissection and the effectiveness in the creative design.

items.title: A Physics-Informed Surrogate Safety Gate for Agentic AI Control of SMT Reflow Soldering in Unmanned-System Electronics Manufacturing: A Simulation-Based Study
items.abstract: Surface mount technology (SMT) assembly lines running under high-mix low-volume (HMLV) conditions face a recurring parameter-optimization problem, because frequent product changeovers invalidate static control recipes and expose the nonlinear coupling between solder paste printing and reflow soldering. A large language model (LLM) can reason about that coupling. Its outputs are probabilistic and its inference latency is network-dependent, so it cannot be wired directly to process actuators. This paper takes that obstacle as its research question. The proposed multilayer Agentic AI and physics-informed digital twin (Agentic AI-DT) framework, a digital-twin architecture evaluated here as a digital model driven by a simulated closed loop, places a cloud-hosted LLM in the strategy role and an edge-deployed conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE), trained with a thermodynamic partial differential equation residual penalty, in the role of a gate that runs the same deterministic check on every strategy before it reaches the reflow oven controller. The check executes deterministically, but its verdicts inherit the surrogate's prediction error, so the safety it provides is measured here and not assumed. The study measures the gate itself: how often it fires, and how often it errs in each direction. A two-stage pipeline combining Latin Hypercube Sampling with singular value decomposition based reduced-order modelling expands 1,000 calibrated finite element simulations into 50,000 training scenarios, and 200 further independent finite element runs form the held-out test set. On those runs the physics-informed CVAE reaches a mean squared error of 1.93 ℃ 2 , 25.2% below a CVAE trained without the physics term and 14.6% below a standalone physics-informed neural network. Across 347 candidate strategies the gate vetoes 63 (18.2%). Finite element re-simulation shows that 5 of the 284 admitted candidates (1.76%, 95% CI 0.8 to 4.1%) were unsafe and that 14 of the 63 vetoed candidates (22.2%, 95% CI 13.7 to 33.9%) were safe, giving 94.5% agreement with the reference solver. Closed-loop profile tracking error is 2.09 ℃, against 3.18 ℃ for model predictive control and 4.62 ℃ for fixed-gain PID. The diagnostic layer names the injected root cause in 84.0% of 300 scripted fault trials, against 72.7% for a random forest classifier and 61.3% for a rule-based expert system. Median end-to-end latency is 419 ms, 90.7% of 2,000 cycles finish inside the 500 ms design budget, and the remaining cycles commit a re-checked last validated setpoint at the 500 ms boundary, reaching the controller within 539 ms. Every number reported here comes from a synthetic environment calibrated against three published sets of measured reflow profiles. No physical production line was instrumented, so these are simulation-fidelity measurements rather than production performance guarantees.

items.title: A proposed HTTPS Like Security Layer for AI agent actions: it asks "will this action do exactly what it was authorized to do?"
items.abstract: The internet already has strong answers for many security questions. TCP/IP delivers data. HTTPS and TLS encrypt the connection and confirm the server’s identity. OAuth grants an application access to an account. Identity systems confirm who a user or workload is. Logs and monitoring record what happened afterwards. Each of these remains essential, and each answers a question about the connection, the identity, or the record. AI agents raise a different question. An agent can now call APIs, send emails, export files, initiate payments, change databases, reconfigure cloud infrastructure, issue network commands, and control physical devices, often in milliseconds and without a human in the loop. A request can travel over a perfectly secure HTTPS connection, carry a valid OAuth token, and come from an authenticated agent, yet carry the wrong amount, the wrong destination, an expired approval, a revoked permission, a replayed request, or an instruction injected into the agent through a malicious prompt. By the time monitoring raises an alert, the payment has settled, the data has left, and the system has changed. This disclosure proposes a security layer above HTTPS that verifies each action at the moment it takes effect. Every action an AI agent proposes is held in a pending state with no external effect. A protected component, outside the agent’s control, checks that specific action against the conditions that apply: who authorized it, for what purpose, to which destination, under which policy version, within which time window, and whether permission has since been revoked. When every check passes, it issues a single-use authorization bound to that exact action and to the specific system that will carry it out. That system, whether an API gateway, payment processor, cloud control plane, network egress gateway, database, or device controller, verifies the authorization and consumes it in the same step as execution. An altered, replayed, expired, or unverified action stays blocked, and alternate routes to the same effect, such as backup systems, debug interfaces, or direct device access, pass through the same check. The layer works alongside HTTPS, OAuth, identity management, and existing access controls, and requires none of them to change. It applies to AI agents and tool calls, cloud operations, payments, telecommunications, and critical infrastructure. HTTPS secures the connection; this layer ensures each action does exactly what it was authorized to do.
